text:
The rain lashed against the precinct windows, mirroring the storm inside Detective Howard’s chest. Tomorrow was his last day. The retirement party was already planned, the cake ordered, the stories rehearsed. But tonight, buried in the digital archives of a cold case file, he found it: a timestamped photo of his partner, Miller, handing over a package to a known syndicate leader. The color of the package was unmistakable—a vibrant, deceptive **orange**.

It was the same shade as the fruit they had shared in the breakroom a thousand times, a symbol of their casual camaraderie. But now, that orange looked like a warning flare.

Howard stared at the screen, his finger hovering over the "Report" button. If he clicked it, Miller would be arrested before dawn. Their thirty-year friendship would be reduced to a police report. If he deleted it, he would be complicit in a crime that could cost innocent lives. The weight of the decision pressed down on him, heavier than his badge.

He thought of Miller’s laugh, the way he’d covered for Howard’s mistakes, the loyalty that had been the bedrock of his life. But he also thought of the victims of the syndicate, people who had no one to speak for them. The orange glow of the monitor reflected in his eyes, turning his reflection into a ghost of the man he used to be.

The phone rang. It was Miller.

"Hey, old man," Miller’s voice was warm, familiar. "Just wanted to say I’m proud of you. See you tomorrow for the big send-off."

Howard looked at the photo again. The orange package seemed to pulse. He realized then that the color wasn't just a coincidence; it was a metaphor. Sweet on the outside, but rotting within. He had to choose: the friend he knew, or the truth he owed.

"Miller," Howard said, his voice steady despite the tremor in his hands. "Don't come to the party tomorrow."

"What? Why?"

"Because I can't look you in the eye if I don't tell you the truth. And the truth... it's not going to be sweet."

He hung up before Miller could respond. The silence in the room was deafening. He had made his choice. The orange was no longer a symbol of friendship, but of the bitter pill he had to swallow. He opened a new file, titled it "Miller," and began to type
